title: Regression and residuals
goals: Calculate signed residuals with a stated convention
Use residual patterns to question a model

prerequisite.prompt: What does a class label predict?
prerequisite.answer: A category; regression predicts a numeric target instead.

vocabulary: Observed target minus predicted target in this course
A prediction below the observed value
A prediction above the observed value

blocks.text: A school garden example predicts plant height in cm from recorded conditions. The target is numeric, so a prediction can be too high or too low by different amounts. Define residual as observed minus predicted. Keep units and the sign convention visible; some software uses the opposite error convention.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines regression and residuals.

Observed heights [4, 7, 9] cm and predictions [5, 6, 9] cm give residuals [-1, 1, 0] cm. The first prediction is too high, the second too low and the third exact. Mean signed residual is zero, yet two predictions are wrong. Opposite errors can cancel.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
observed = [4, 7, 9]
predicted = [5, 6, 9]
residuals = [y - p for y, p in zip(observed, predicted)]
print(residuals)
print(sum(residuals) / len(residuals))
# Output: [-1, 1, 0] and 0.0.
# Opposite signed errors can cancel.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Regression and residuals at a glance
blocks.caption: To inspect a residual plot, place a feature or prediction on the horizontal axis and residual on the vertical axis. A trend can suggest a missed relationship. It does not by itself identify the cause or validate a new model. Use development data for analysis and preserve an independent final test.

blocks.label: Why does mean residual zero not imply perfect predictions? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: If predictions for early, middle and late growth have residuals -2, 0, 3 cm, the model moves from overpredicting to underpredicting across those records. Investigate whether a straight-line assumption or a missing condition could explain it. Check measurement consistency before adding complexity.

A residual of zero is an agreement with the measured target, not proof that the measurement is perfect. Do not compare errors measured in cm directly with errors measured in metres. Keep the same row pairing, unit and sign convention throughout.

blocks.label: A report combines 2 cm and .02 m as if they were different magnitudes. Repair it.

workbook.title: Calculate residuals
workbook.prompt: Compute the worked residuals and identify overprediction.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals -1, 1, 0 cm; the first record is overpredicted.

workbook.title: Explain cancellation
workbook.prompt: Why does mean residual zero not imply perfect predictions?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Negative and positive residuals cancel even when individual errors are nonzero.

workbook.title: Read a pattern
workbook.prompt: Interpret residuals -2, 0, 3 ordered by growth stage.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: They shift from overprediction to underprediction; investigate a missed relationship without claiming a proven cause.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Observed [6, 10, 13], predicted [8, 9, 11] cm. Give residuals, mean residual and error directions.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals [-2, 1, 2] cm; mean 1/3 cm. First overpredicted, others underpredicted.

workbook.title: Check units
workbook.prompt: A report combines 2 cm and .02 m as if they were different magnitudes. Repair it.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Convert to a shared unit; both represent 2 cm. Document units before comparing or aggregating errors.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. This week focuses on regression and residuals. Model the worked example first, collect the new W 4 case independently before feedback, and use the fresh retry to check transfer. Award credit for traceable reasoning and bounded claims, including justified uncertainty.
materials: Paper, pencils and a calculator for fractions
The fictional examples and a blank evidence table
Optional Python 3 editor; no external packages or AI accounts required
sessions: Use the prerequisite question: What does a class label predict? Check the explanation before proceeding.

Read the visual row by row. Collect the guided explanation and compare reasoning in pairs. Trace the Python check after the paper calculation.
Retrieve the distinction between regression and residual. Invite a counterexample to an overconfident claim.
Discuss the application and complete W 3: Interpret residuals -2, 0, 3 ordered by growth stage.
Collect W4 independently before giving hints. Assess these outcomes: Distinguish numeric prediction from classification; Calculate signed residuals with a stated convention. Record any support used.

teacher.assessment: For independent W 4, require: Residuals [-2, 1, 2] cm; mean 1/3 cm. First overpredicted, others underpredicted. Fresh retry observed [3, 8, 12], predicted [4, 8, 10]: residuals [-1, 0, 2], mean 1/3 in the target unit. Require sign interpretations. Mark each criterion as independent, supported or not yet demonstrated. Reassess the reasoning after feedback; do not replace the first attempt silently.

Use regression and residual in full sentences. Extension: alter one condition in the worked example and explain which conclusion changes and which remains supported.
